The National Research Lab program

NRL 2.0 is a national program jointly administered by the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Science and ICT to develop university-affiliated research institutes. Selected in 2026, SNU Robotics Institute undertakes the Human-centered Physical AI Robotics (H-PAIR) Institute project with support for up to ten years. NRL is a research program within SNU Robotics Institute, bringing together researchers from engineering, medicine, public health, brain and cognitive sciences, and the social sciences.

Research Goals

Through this program, SNU Robotics Institute develops foundational technologies for human-centered physical AI by co-designing robot bodies and intelligence. Concentrating all decisions and control in a central AI creates challenges in computation, energy use and response time in complex real-world settings. The project combines embodied physical intelligence, in which materials, structures, contact and deformation contribute to computation and adaptation, with distributed intelligence, in which local modules process information, learn and cooperate with higher-level intelligence. The goal is to establish design, learning and control principles for robots that adapt to their environments and users.

Human-centered research addresses both robot capabilities and the conditions in which people use them. Safety, clinical reliability, user autonomy and social acceptance are considered and assessed from the design stage. Digital twins of robot–human–environment interactions complement physical experiments to evaluate performance and practical applicability.

Research framework: Technology Cores and Project Groups

Technology Cores (TCs) develop foundational technologies shared across applications. Project Groups (PGs) define use environments and research requirements, then apply and evaluate these technologies.

Technology Core

  • TC 1 MORPHI Body

    Adaptive robot bodies using the physical properties of materials and structures

  • TC 2 MOSAIC Intelligence

    Distributed intelligence coordinating local and global modules

  • TC 3 Digital Twin

    Robot–human–environment models for design, learning and evaluation

  • TC 4 Human Value

    Assessment of safety, clinical reliability and social acceptance

Project Group

  • PG 1 Life Companion

    Everyday assistance robots that adapt to user intentions and changing living environments

  • PG 2 Wearable

    Wearable robots that assist or augment movement, strength and balance

  • PG 3 Intra-Body

    Robots and diagnostic or therapeutic interfaces operating inside the human body

Validation and translation

The program aims to apply foundational technologies in realistic settings and use the results to guide further development. Shared fabrication, data and computing infrastructure supports this work. A Lab-to-Market framework connects research with industry collaboration, technology commercialization and entrepreneurship.

Technology Core

Research on adaptive robot materials and structures, distributed intelligence, digital twins, and safety and social acceptance.

TC 01 · MORPHI BODY

Adaptive Robot Materials, Structures and Physical Intelligence

Why it matters

Robots that move in contact with people must respond safely to unpredictable changes. Handling every response through sensors and complex control algorithms increases computation and energy demand. Materials and structures that distribute forces and adapt mechanically to their surroundings can help overcome the limitations of a fixed robot body.

Research approach

MORPHI Body combines physical intelligence with structures that change shape and stiffness. Mechanisms are designed to find balance and distribute forces, allowing the body itself to perform part of the computation and control. We also study how robots sense their own physical state and respond to bodily changes, aiming for safe interaction and affordable, energy-efficient hardware.

Key research topics

  • Reconfigurable actuation and structures: joints with actively adjustable shape and stiffness, and bio-inspired artificial muscles
  • Self-sensing skin: soft distributed tactile sensors and systems for monitoring the robot’s physical state
  • Modularity and reliability: shared specifications and durability and reliability evaluation for low-cost, low-power hardware

TC 02 · MOSAIC INTELLIGENCE

Cooperative Distributed Intelligence and Continual Learning

Why it matters

Retraining an entire intelligence system whenever a robot’s body or task environment changes demands substantial time and computing resources. Real-world interaction also requires immediate responses to contact and changing conditions. Robots therefore need an architecture that can learn and reconfigure individual functions while coordinating overall behavior.

Research approach

Inspired by functional specialization and coordination in the brain, MOSAIC Intelligence organizes local intelligence modules under a contextual global intelligence. Local modules learn physical interactions and movement, while global intelligence interprets situations and goals and coordinates their cooperation. We study module recomposition and continual learning across both levels to enable efficient adaptation to different bodies and tasks.

Key research topics

  • Autonomous local intelligence: modules that perceive robot–human–environment physical properties and learn movement independently
  • Contextual global intelligence: understanding and predicting situations to coordinate perception and movement modules
  • Continual learning and co-evolution: local and global intelligence learning together and adapting to new environments and missions

TC 03 · ROBOT–HUMAN–ENVIRONMENT DIGITAL TWIN

Robot–Human–Environment Digital Twin

Why it matters

Predicting contact between people and robots in changing environments requires multiple physical phenomena to be considered together. Existing digital twins can be fragmented by phenomenon, or face a trade-off between prediction accuracy and computing speed. Faster robot design, learning and validation require accurate, rapid simulation alongside consistent management of diverse data.

Research approach

The Robot–Human–Environment Digital Twin connects multiphysics simulation, a data fabric and integrated software–hardware optimization. We study how to generate and augment physically consistent data in virtual experiments and connect it with real-world observations for iterative robot design and validation. The aim is an integrated framework that supports everyday assistance, wearable and in-body robotics under their different operating conditions.

Key research topics

  • Digital twin: high-accuracy, high-speed simulation of physical interactions and generation of data for learning and validation
  • Data fabric: generating, augmenting, storing and managing large-scale multimodal data while preserving physical consistency and context
  • Infrastructure optimization: integrated software–hardware design for efficient simulation and data processing

TC 04 · HUMAN VALUE

Robot Safety, Clinical Reliability and Social Acceptance

Why it matters

Higher performance alone does not make a robot beneficial or trustworthy. Robots that directly affect people’s bodies and daily lives must account for human values, including safety, functioning and autonomy. Rather than relying only on ethics or user evaluations after development, these values need to inform design, control and real-world validation from the outset.

Research approach

Human Value studies a Value Operating System (Value OS) that translates human-centered values into design decisions and control principles that can be verified throughout development. Scenarios reflecting clinical and social contexts are used to examine robot behavior and risks to human values, with findings fed back into subsequent designs. This supports consistent assessment of clinical reliability and social acceptance.

Key research topics

  • Value-based design: defining indicators for safety, functioning and autonomy and using them in design and validation
  • Demonstration and stress testing: identifying thresholds of value compromise across interaction scenarios and explaining assessment results
  • Shared criteria and design feedback: studying a Human Value API and trust criteria, and feeding evaluation results into control and design improvements

PG 01 · LIFE COMPANION

Robots for Everyday Assistance

We study robots that understand human intentions and environmental changes, and share everyday tasks in open, unstructured settings such as homes and living spaces.

  • Adaptive bodies and movement that respond to changes in people and spaces
  • Intelligence and interaction informed by context and user needs
  • Methods for iterative learning and validation in real living environments

PG 02 · WEARABLE

Wearable Robots for Movement Assistance and Augmentation

Robots worn directly on the body support movement, strength and balance, providing a natural experience tailored to each person’s physical characteristics.

  • Assistive technologies that respond to body movement and user intent
  • Personalized designs that balance comfort and actuation performance
  • Design and evaluation informed by human–robot interaction data

PG 03 · INTRA-BODY

Robots Operating Inside the Human Body

We develop robots and interfaces that operate in harmony with surrounding tissue in confined, sensitive internal environments, and build validation frameworks connected to clinical practice.

  • Soft, adaptive structures for confined and complex environments
  • Precise motion that accounts for interactions between robots and biological environments
  • Demonstration and evaluation methods grounded in safety and clinical reliability
